articles.title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
articles.excerpt: When our AI code reviewer's cost per run doubled, we dug into the token usage to find out why. Learn how we used prompt caching and intelligent model routing to slash our inference bill by 68% while speeding up reviews.
details: When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April , an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave.
Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them - aggressively.
With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started.
Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before.
About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in.

articles.title: How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code
articles.excerpt: Learn how to move an agent session from the GitHub Copilot app into VS Code without losing the conversation, code changes, or working context. The post How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it.

But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app ... and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code?

You don't. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing.
Push your updates to the pull request associated with the session.
Visual Studio Code installed and connected to the same GitHub account.

articles.title: Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models
articles.excerpt: Clairic is a new model from Cloudflare that is a System One extraction modeI, capable of extracting, computing, estimating, and forecasting data from unstructured inputs.
details: Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models.
Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic.

Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs - all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs.
When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm.

As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow , a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs).

articles.title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
articles.excerpt: Following the discovery that eight eMudhra intermediate certificates use weak keys, Cloudflare is deploying mitigations and releasing client updates. We explain the impact, our response, and what customers and developers should do next.
details: On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised.
These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare.
Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic.
This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet.
For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

articles.title: Introducing tsrs: A port of TypeScript to Rust
articles.excerpt: Cloudflare is collaborating on tsrs, a Rust port of TypeScript that is up to 8x faster and uses 70% less memory.
details: Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs , a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain .

Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser.

To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that.
The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation.
A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible.

articles.title: A fully programmable secure web gateway
articles.excerpt: Cloudflare Gateway and Data Loss Prevention have inherited the flexibility and power of Cloudflare Workers through our full-stack integration with the Cloudflare Developer platform.
details: Every secure web gateway on the market works the same way: traffic matches a condition. A terminal action fires. Allow, Block, Isolate, Log. This model has been the foundation of network security for nearly 30 years, and it handles the common case well. But it has a ceiling, and customers with complex environments hit that ceiling regularly.
Earlier this year, we shared our vision to build a truly programmable SASE platform .
We also outlined how the term programmability has become diluted by the security industry.
Most vendors claim programmability because they have public APIs, Terraform providers, webhooks, and alerting.
Cloudflare offers all of those things too, but that’s not enough.

articles.title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
articles.excerpt: CVE-2026-88771 lets attackers run commands on NetScaler Gateway before anyone signs in. Patching takes time most teams don't have, so the sign-in decision has to move in front of the vulnerable code.
details: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server.
Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in.
As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update.

If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls.

This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server?

articles.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
articles.excerpt: Three Java Champions share how they use GitHub Copilot to solve problems, accelerate development, and keep humans responsible for the results. The post How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships.

To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software.

Patrick Baumgartner , software crafter at 42talents with 20+ years of Java experience
Frank Delporte , senior technical writer at Azul and maintainer of Foojay.io with 15+ years of Java experience

articles.title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
articles.excerpt: Identity alone doesn't guarantee a bot will behave responsibly. We are introducing a system to continuously evaluate whether Verified bots honor site preferences, like robots.txt and HTTP 429s, ensuring they remain accountable over time.
details: A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious - often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug.

Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm .
Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.”

articles.title: Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org
articles.excerpt: Put native GitHub features to work to review outside collaborator access and archive stale repositories. The post Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they've served their purpose.

To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer.

We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees ("Hubbers") collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen , a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization.
Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows:
Outside collaborator access reviews. Every quarter, each repo's outside collaborators are reviewed. Keep who you need, and everyone else is removed.
